title: Week 30 Check-In · By the Great Horn Spoon!
description: This week you finished the novel with Chapters 16 to 18 and looked back at the whole book. You practiced editing for punctuation, capitalization and clarity, reviewed root families from the unit, edited for spelling, saw how the parts of a poem combine to make meaning, and wrote and published the conclusion of your adventure.

questions.label: Key Event
questions.text: How do Praiseworthy and Jack find their gold?
options: They follow Dr. Buckbee’s map to its X-mark.
They dig a grave the Justice of the Peace ordered, and hit bedrock.
Pitch-pine Billy tells them where to dig.

questions.label: Character
questions.text: Why does Praiseworthy speak up for Cut-Eye Higgins at Shirt-tail Camp?
options: He wants to be the camp’s lawyer.
He gave his word as part of a bargain, and he stands by it.
questions.from: 30.1 Reading Q1 (Ch. 16: “He’d given his word and he had to stand by it.”)

questions.label: Theme
questions.text: Near the end, Praiseworthy says this line. Explain how it works as a proposal of marriage and as a way to sum up the whole gold rush story.
questions.excerpt: “Maybe this isn’t the time or the place, Miss Arabella, but when a man strikes gold he doesn’t lose any time staking a claim.”
questions.key: Staking a claim means quickly marking what you have found so no one else takes it; Praiseworthy has ‘struck gold’ in Arabella and wants to claim her first. It sums up the story because the partners came for gold but the real treasure is the family.
questions.status: fixed (the line is now quoted exactly)

questions.label: Poetry
questions.text: In “Eldorado,” why does the word shadow come back in every stanza?
options: It ties the stanzas together and grows darker as the knight’s search goes on.
It is the name of the knight’s horse.
It shows that the whole poem happens at night.

questions.label: Your Conclusion
questions.text: Copy the last two or three sentences of your published adventure. Then explain in one sentence how your ending connects the adventure, your hero, and what the story means.
questions.key: The student’s ending plus one sentence naming how it ties together what happened, how the hero changed, and the story’s meaning.

passage.title: Reading passage (Chapter 16)
passage.text: They chose a bare spot about half a mile from camp. It was on a bluff covered with oat straw and overlooking the river. They pulled pick and shovel from Stubb’s pack ropes and set to work. “Fine-looking country, isn’t it?” Praiseworthy muttered. “Even to be buried in.” Jack tried not to think about Boston. It would soon be time to start back and all they had to show for their labors was a worthless map. Poor Aunt Arabella, he thought. They would lose the house for sure. The entire trip to California was beginning to look like a wild-goose chase. When they got the hole four feet deep they couldn’t go any farther. They hit bedrock. And struck gold.
passage.cite: Sid Fleischman, By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 16
